newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM seeking closer, broader ASEAN ties.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM seeking closer, broader ASEAN ties.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto flies to Brunei on Tuesday to kick off a five-nation Southeast Asian trip aimed at adding a political dimension to Tokyo's strong trade and investment ties to the region.

Keeping one eye on the protracted hostage standoff at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru, Hashimoto will call for regular top-level dialogue between Japan and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), foreign ministry officials said.

"I would like to deepen that relationship. I think it would be a good idea if there was a forum where the leaders of ASEAN and Japan could regularly talk things over face to face," the prime minister told a news conference at the weekend.

Over eight days, Hashimoto will meet with the leaders of Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Singapore. Japan's two-way trade with those five nations totalled $74 billion in 1995, while Tokyo's cumulative investment stood at $33 billion, according to foreign ministry figures.
Hashimoto visited the other two members of ASEAN, the Philippines and Thailand, last year.
"The visit presents an important chance to realise a broadened Japan-ASEAN relationship and to explore areas in which the two partners can work together," said a senior foreign ministry official.
In a policy speech to be delivered on January 14 in Singapore, the 59-year-old prime minister will unveil what aides have dubbed the "Hashimoto doctrine", spelling out Japan's Asia-Pacific policy.

Japan intends to engage the nations of ASEAN, which celebrates its 30th anniversary this year, as an "equal partner" in dialogue along the lines of contacts established between the European Union and ASEAN, the officials said.
The four pillars of the policy are political dialogue and security, cultural exchange, economic aid and cooperation and joint efforts to combat global problems, officials said.

Topping Hashimoto's security agenda will be his effort to update ASEAN leaders on Japan-U.S. moves to consolidate U.S. military bases on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa while stepping up bilateral security cooperation in the region.

It was not clear to what extent Hashimoto would raise the delicate issue of China's political and military ambitions in the region, a concern shared -- but seldom voiced -- by Japan or the ASEAN countries.
Hashimoto will also convey Japan's willingness to help tackle environmental problems and energy shortages spawned by the region's booming economic growth.

In a sign that Hashimoto will deal delicately with his ASEAN hosts' approach to human rights and other contentious issues, the Japanese prime minister on Monday avoided a meeting in Tokyo with East Timor activist and Nobel laureate Jose Ramos Horta, citing a busy schedule.
Horta at a news conference urged Hashimoto to be "very forceful in raising the issue of human rights" in his meeting with Indonesian President Suharto on Friday.
On Tuesday Hashimoto will meet Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, Brunei's prime minister and defence minister, followed by a Wednesday meeting with Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad.

After meeting with Suharto, Hashimoto is to fly to Vietnam on Saturday to meet Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and Communist Party General Secretary Do Muoi. He wraps up the visit with talks with Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong on Monday.
